Se toma como población la que dan tus da: The population is taken to be the one given by your data and 100 samples of the same size are drawn. Each line is the interval of one sample: green if it contains the true value and red if not.
Con una muestra se estima un parámetro d: A sample is used to estimate a population parameter (the mean μ, a proportion p, the variance σ<sup>2</sup>…). A 95 % confidence interval is an interval calculated with a method that is right, that is, contains the true value, in 95 % of samples. That is why the simulation shows about 95 green intervals out of every 100. The confidence level is 1 − α, and α is the probability of failing, split between two tails of α/2.

If σ is unknown, it is replaced by the sample standard deviation s (the one that divides by n − 1) and z by Student's t with n − 1 degrees of freedom, t<sub>n−1; α/2</sub>. For large n the two give almost the same.

Ese intervalo normal (de Wald) es el de: That normal (Wald) interval is the classroom one, but it fails with few successes or failures: it can go outside [0, 1] or collapse to a point. There are three alternatives. Wilson solves for p from the inequality instead of estimating the error with p̂ and works well for any n. The exact Clopper-Pearson comes from the binomial itself and guarantees at least the requested confidence, at the cost of being somewhat wider. Agresti-Coull is the usual normal one after adding z² observations, half of them successes (at 95 %, “add 2 successes and 2 failures”).

Y si se quiere un intervalo que contenga: And if you want an interval containing a proportion of the whole population (for example, 90 % of the parts), it is a tolerance interval x̄ ± k·s, with a factor k that depends on n, the proportion and the confidence. Both assume the population is normal and, unlike that of the mean, they do not shrink to zero as the sample grows.

To halve the error you need four times as large a sample.
